name: Wellington Management
reason: Public AI content is investment commentary — AI as a theme to invest in — not internal adoption. The only substantive public account of its internal quantitative platform predates 2023, outside this dashboard's evidence window.

name: Point72
reason: Initially listed, withdrawn on human review: available reporting was dated or described support of external businesses rather than current internal adoption.

name: New York State Common Retirement Fund
reason: Public AI activity is stewardship engagement with portfolio companies and the Comptroller's audits of other state agencies — not the Fund's own investment operations.

name: Apollo Global Management
reason: The public AI record is AI-infrastructure financing, portfolio-company AI programs, and an AI-services venture — all excluded by scope. No public evidence of AI inside Apollo's own investment process.

name: Marshall Wace
reason: The 2023+ public record shows adoption of an ML-priced vendor data feed and disclosures about AI-related costs — neither is an internal AI use case. Pre-2023 quantitative heritage is outside the evidence window.

name: D. E. Shaw & Co.
reason: One qualifying dated event (a generative-AI human-capital function, 2025). The would-be second event rests solely on an outlet outside the accepted source list — below the two-event minimum.

name: Baillie Gifford
reason: The only public internal-adoption account is a sponsored, firm-authored article, which the sourcing rules exclude as a sole source. Own-domain AI content is investment-thesis commentary.

name: Walleye Capital
reason: A single strong 2026 vendor-published event (firm-wide AI coding-assistant adoption) with no independent second source — below the two-event minimum. Revisited if independent coverage lands.

name: QIA (Qatar Investment Authority)
reason: Extensive public AI activity — stakes in AI companies and AI-infrastructure ventures — is investment exposure, which scope excludes. No public evidence of AI inside QIA's own investment process.

name: Khazanah Nasional
reason: Public AI signals are AI-sector investments and national AI-policy research; the fund's own disclosures contain no internal-adoption claim.

name: Robeco
reason: Initially listed, withdrawn on human review: the public record covers AI governance and AI in client-facing products rather than adoption inside the firm's own investment process.

name: APG

name: PFA Pension
reason: Production signal does not come from investments decision. all news are out of date thus no staging.

name: IMC Trading
reason: Unclear about use cases from public domain. All present tense production claim is undated.

name: Harvard Management Company
reason: Its own FY2024 and FY2025 annual reports contain no mention of artificial intelligence, machine learning or data science; its website carries no AI-related news, careers or process content; and Chief Investment Officer's full coverage archive records only returns, allocation, restructuring and governance. The only AI connections found are portfolio holdings and a venture stake, which are out of scope as an investment thesis rather than operational use. No qualifying evidence of internal operational adoption was found. Its own job board is script-rendered and could not be read, so hiring signals remain unchecked.

name: Princeton University Investment Company (PRINCO)
reason: Every page of its website was checked — it publishes no news, press or insights section — and none describes AI, machine learning or data science in its investment process; it describes its edge as analytic and judgmental. Chief Investment Officer's full coverage archive back to 2017 carries no AI content. The only AI references on its own domain are a staff member's pre-hire academic thesis and the university's research funding priorities, neither of which is PRINCO's own operations. Trade-press search endpoints could not be reached, so that channel is unchecked.

name: William and Flora Hewlett Foundation
reason: Its entire public AI record is grantmaking to outside institutions — the $100 million Emerging Technology and Security Initiative announced in July 2026 and its predecessor cyber programme — which is AI the foundation funds others to build and adopt, not AI in its own operations. No dated evidence of internal adoption was found across its newsroom and reporting on it, and the foundation is not named anywhere in the Center for Effective Philanthropy's sector survey of foundation AI use, including its funder acknowledgements. One staff blog returned an access error and the audited financials did not extract, so both remain unchecked.
